module.title: Mathematical Reasoning & Discrete Foundations
module.destination: State claims precisely, prove/refute them, reason with sets/maps, and execute deterministic finite counting before probability.
module.gate: Page completion is not clearance. Every ownership claim has exact public-request/rubric evidence; universal proof tasks require general reasoning.

sessions.title: Mathematical statements, truth values & predicates
sessions.purpose: Build mathematical statements, truth values & predicates as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Distinguish a truth-evaluable statement from an expression/question. Determine a closed statement's truth value. Distinguish an open predicate from a closed statement. Identify a predicate's free variable. Evaluate a predicate at a supplied input.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for mathematical statements, truth values & predicates.

Determine a closed statement's truth value.
Distinguish an open predicate from a closed statement.

sessions.lesson: A statement is a complete sentence that is true or false; expressions and questions are not statements, while a predicate becomes closed only after its free variable is supplied or quantified. Worked example: “9 is odd” is a true statement; “u+7” is an expression; “u>7” is a predicate. Guided check: Classify “2+5=8”, “v²−1”, and “v²=1”, then evaluate the predicate at v=1 and v=3.

sessions.lesson: P→Q fails only at P=true,Q=false. Converse is Q→P; inverse ¬P→¬Q; contrapositive ¬Q→¬P; original and contrapositive are equivalent. Worked example: x>6→x>2 is true over reals, but the converse fails at x=4. Guided check: Write all four forms of x<−1→x<3.

sessions.lesson: P↔Q means both P→Q and Q→P. If P→Q, P is sufficient for Q and Q necessary for P; the reverse needs separate proof. Worked example: x=5 is sufficient for x²=25, but x²=25 is not sufficient for x=5 because x=−5 also works. Guided check: Compare x=0 with |x|=0.

sessions.title: Universal & existential quantifiers
sessions.purpose: Build universal & existential quantifiers as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: State the quantifier domain. Interpret universal quantification. Interpret existential quantification. Use a witness for an existential. Use a counterexample against a universal.

sessions.lesson: ∀ requires every legal value; ∃ requires at least one. A witness establishes an existential; one legal counterexample refutes a universal. Worked example: Over integers, ∃n(n²=9) has witness3, while ∀n(n>−100) is false. Guided check: Decide ∀n(n²≥0) and ∃n(n²=16) over integers.

sessions.lesson: Negation switches ∀↔∃, negates the predicate, and keeps the same domain. The negation of u>3 is u≤3. Worked example: The negation of 'every real x has x²>1' is 'some real x has x²≤1.' Guided check: Negate 'there exists an integer n with n<−4.'

sessions.title: Mathematical induction

sessions.lesson: Induction verifies a base case, assumes the claim at arbitrary k, uses that assumption to reach k+1, then concludes all cases from the start. Worked example: The sum1+2+…+n can be proved n(n+1)/2 by adding k+1 to the assumed k-case. Guided check: Prove1+…+n<n² for n≥2.

sessions.lesson: Strong induction assumes every earlier case through k, never k+1 itself. It is useful when a new case depends on multiple or non-immediate earlier cases. Worked example: Representing sufficiently large integers using2s and3s can use several base cases and an earlier reduction. Guided check: Identify base cases for a recurrence depending on the two previous terms.
